text: In the centre of the studio, clamped to an upright easel, stood the full-length portrait of a young man of extraordinary personal beauty
speaker: C1

text: and in front of it, some little distance away, stood the artist himself, Basil Hallward
speaker: C2

text: Whose sudden disappearance some years ago caused public excitement. And gave rise to many strange conjectures.
speaker: C2

text: His friend, Lord Henery Wotton lounged nearby observing the artist.
speaker: C4

text: It is your best work, the best thing you have ever done. You must certainly send it next year to the Grosvenor.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: I don't think I shall send it anywhere.
speaker: Basil

text: My dear fellow, why? What odd chaps you painters are! You do anything in the world to gain a reputation.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: As soon as you have one, you seem to want to throw it away.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: I know you will laugh at me but I really can't exhibit it. I have put too much of myself into it.
speaker: Basil

text: Upon my word, Basil, I didn't know you were so vain! I really can't see any resemblance between you and this young Adonis.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Why, he is a Narcissus, and you--well, of course you have an intellectual expression and all that. But beauty, real beauty, ends where an intellectual expression begins.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Intellect is in itself a mode of exaggeration, and destroys the harmony of any face. Don't flatter yourself. You are not in the least like him.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Of course I am not like him. Indeed, I should be sorry to look like him. It is better not to be different from one’s fellows. Your rank and wealth, Harry; my brains, such as they are, my art, whatever it may be worth;
speaker: Basil

text: Dorian Gray's good looks — we shall all suffer for what the gods have given us, suffer terribly.
speaker: Basil

text: Dorian Gray? Is that his name?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Yes, that is his name. I didn't intend to tell it to you.
speaker: Basil

text: But why not?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: When I like people immensely, I never tell their names to anyone. It is like surrendering a part of them. I have grown to love secrecy. When I leave town now I never tell my people where I am going.
speaker: Basil

text: If I did, I would lose all my pleasure. I suppose you think me awfully foolish about it?
speaker: Basil

text: Not at all, my dear Basil. You seem to forget that I am married, and the one charm of marriage is that it makes a life of deception absolutely necessary for both parties.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: I never know where my wife is and my wife never knows what I'm doing.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: I hate the way you talk about your married life, Harry. I believe that you are really a very good husband, but that you are thoroughly ashamed of your own virtues. Your cynicism is simply a pose.
speaker: Basil

text: Being natural is simply a pose, and the most irritating pose I know. I am afraid I must be going, but before I do, I want you to explain to me why you won't exhibit Dorian Gray's picture.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Harry, every portrait that is painted with feeling is a portrait of the artist. It is not the sitter who is revealed by the painter; it is rather the painter who reveals himself. I’m afraid that I have shown in this picture the secret of my own soul.
speaker: Basil

text: And what is that?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Lord Henery felt as if he could hear Basil's heart beating.
speaker: C1

text: And wondered what was coming.
speaker: C2

text: Two months ago I went to a crush at Lady Brandon's.
speaker: Basil

text: Well, I suddenly became conscious that someone was looking at me. I turned half-way round and saw Dorian Gray for the first time. When our eyes met a curious sensation of terror came over me.
speaker: Basil

text: I knew that I had come face to face with someone whose mere personality was so fascinating that, if I allowed it to do so, it would absorb my whole nature, my whole soul, my very art itself. I had a strange feeling that fate had in store for me exquisite joys and exquisite sorrows.
speaker: Basil

text: I grew afraid and turned to quit the room. I struggled to the door. There, of course, I stumbled against Lady Brandon.
speaker: Basil

text: You are not going to run away so soon, Mr. Hallward?
speaker: Lady B

text: She screamed out. You know her curiously shrill voice?
speaker: Basil

text: Yes; she is a peacock in everything but beauty.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: I could not get rid of her.

text: She brought him up to royalties,

text: She brought me up to a truculent red faced old gentleman covered all over with orders and ribbons, hissing into my ear in a tragic whisper that must have been heard by all.

text: Although I had only met her once before. Suddenly I found myself face to face with the young man whose personality had so strangely stirred me. Our eyes met again. It was reckless of me, but I asked Lady Brandon to introduce me to him.

text: Charming boy - poor dear mother and I - absolutely inseparable. Quite forget what he does - afraid he doesn't do anything - oh, yes, plays the piano - or is it the violin, dear Mr.Gray?

text: Neither of us could help laughing, and we became friends at once.
speaker: Basil

text: Laughter is not at all a bad beginning for a friendship, and it is by far the best ending for one.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: You don't understand what friendship is, Harry or what enmity is, for that matter. You are indifferent to everyone.
speaker: Basil

text: How horribly unjust of you. I make a great difference between people. I choose my friends for their good looks, my acquaintances for their good characters, and my enemies for their good intellects.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: According to your category, I must be a mere acquaintance.
speaker: Basil

text: Oh but you are much more than an acquaintance.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: And much less than a friend. A sort of brother I suppose.
speaker: Basil

text: I don't care for brothers. My elder brother won't die and my younger brothers never seem to do anything else. But tell me more about Mr Gray. How often do you see him?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Every day. I couldn't be happy if I didn't see him every day. He is absolutely necessary to me.
speaker: Basil

text: I thought you would never care for anything but your art.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: He is all my art to me now. He is much more to me than a model or a sitter. His personality has suggested to me an entirely new manner in art, an entirely new mode of style with all the passion of the romantic spirit, the harmony of soul and body.
speaker: Basil

text: We in our madness have separated the two, and have invented a realism that is vulgar, an ideality that is void. If you only knew what Dorian is to me!
speaker: Basil

text: While I was painting that landscape of mine, he sat beside me. Some subtle influence passed from him to me, and for the first time in my life I saw in the plain woodland the wonder I had always looked for and always missed.
speaker: Basil

text: This is extraordinary! I must see this young man who has caused such a stir in your soul.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Dorian is to me simply a motive in art. You might see nothing in him. I see everything in him. I find in him the curves of certain lines, in the loveliness and subtleties of certain colours.
speaker: Basil

text: Then why won't you exhibit his portrait?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Because, without intending it, I have put into it some expression of all this curious artistic idolatry. He must never know anything about it. But the world might guess it, and I will not bare my soul to their shallow prying eyes.
speaker: Basil

text: My heart shall never be put under their microscope. There is too much of myself in the thing, Harry - too much of myself!
speaker: Basil

text: Curious artistic idolatry? Tell me, is Mr Gray also very fond of you?
speaker: Lord Henery

text: He likes me, I know he likes me. Of course I flatter him dreadfully. I find a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I will be sorry for having said. Now and then, however, he is horribly thoughtless, and seems to take a real delight in giving me pain.
speaker: Basil

text: Then I feel, Harry, that I have given away my whole soul to someone who treats it as if it were a flower to put in his coat, a bit of decoration to charm his vanity, an ornament for a summer's day.
speaker: Basil

text: Days in summer, Basil, are apt to linger, Perhaps you will tire sooner than he will. It will be a great pity, for it will alter you. What you have told me is quite a romance, a romance of art one might call it, and the worst of having a romance of any kind is that it leaves one so unromantic.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Don't talk like that. As long as I live, the personality of Dorian Gray will dominate me. You can't feel what I feel. You change too often.
speaker: Basil

text: Ah, my dear Basil, that is exactly why I can feel it. Those who are faithful know only the trivial side of love: it is the faithless who know love's tragedies.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Now I have stayed long enough to miss a dreadful luncheon with my Aunt where the conversation would have been about feeding the poor. My dear fellow, I have just remembered where I heard the name of Dorian Gray.

text: Where? Where was it?

speaker: Dorian

text: If Dorian wishes it, of course you must stay, Harry. Dorian’s whims are laws to everybody, except himself. Stay, Harry, to oblige Dorian, and to oblige me. And now please get up on the platform, and don't pay any attention to what Harry says. He has a very bad influence over all his friends, with the single exception of myself.
speaker: Basil

text: Have you really a very bad influence, Lord Henery? As bad as Basil says?
speaker: Dorian

text: There is no such thing as a good influence. All influence is immoral - immoral from the scientific point of view.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Why?
speaker: Dorian

text: Because to influence a person is to give him one's own soul. He does not think his natural thoughts, or burn with his natural passions. His virtues are not real to him. His sins, if there are such things as sins, are borrowed. People are afraid of themselves, nowadays. They have forgotten the highest of all duties, the duty that one owes to one's self.
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Just turn your head a little more to the right, Dorian, like a good boy.
speaker: Basil

text: Every impulse that we strive to strangle broods in the mind and poisons us. The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it. Resist it, and your soul grows sick with longing for the things it has forbidden to itself, with desire for what its monstrous laws have made monstrous and unlawful. You, Mr. Gray, you yourself, with your rose-red youth and your rose-white boyhood, you have had passions that have made you afraid, thoughts that have filled you with terror, day-dreams and sleeping dreams whose mere memory might stain your cheek with shame…
speaker: Lord Henery

text: Stop! you bewilder me. I don't know what to say. There is some answer to you, but I cannot find it. Don’t speak. Let me think. Or, rather, let me try not to think.
speaker: Dorian

text: For nearly ten minutes he stood there, motionless, with parted lips and eyes strangely bright.

speaker: Lord Henery

text: I don't feel that.
speaker: Dorian

text: No, you don't feel it now. Some day, when you are old and wrinkled and ugly, when thought has seared your forehead with its lines, and passion branded your lips with its hideous fires, you will feel it, you will feel it terribly. You have a wonderfully beautiful face, Mr. Gray. The gods have been good to you. But what the gods give they quickly take away. When your youth goes, your beauty will go with it. Time is jealous of you. You will become sallow, and hollow-cheeked, and dull-eyed. Live! Live the wonderful life that is in you! Let nothing be lost upon you. Be always searching for new sensations. Be afraid of nothing. The moment I met you I saw that you were quite unconscious of what you really are, of what you really might be. I thought how tragic it would be if you were wasted. For there is such a little time that your youth will last - such a little time. We degenerate into hideous puppets, haunted by the memory of the passions of which we were too much afraid, and the exquisite temptations that we had not the courage to yield to. Youth! There is absolutely nothing in the world but youth!
speaker: Lord Henery
